prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B005 alone, with Katori and Ye. After reading all eight statements I am more confident, not less, because the exchange has produced the one-sentence answer the chair asks for. The comb counts the cycles of light, and single-ion clocks control one particle very well. The lattice clock rests on a separate idea. At the magic wavelength the trapping light shifts both clock levels equally, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held tightly (Lamb-Dicke regime) with no Doppler, recoil or first-order Stark shift. That is why the statistical power of many atoms and the systematic control of a trapped particle can be combined, and it is a different mechanism from either earlier prize. It is a conceptual advance and not only a gain in averaging: without the magic condition the many atoms could not be used at all, because the trap itself would destroy the accuracy. The consequences are measured and not promised: about 1e-18 uncertainty, gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres, tightened limits on varying constants and on ultralight dark-matter couplings, and routine comparisons between JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and NPL. As a theorist I add that magic wavelengths and the blackbody shift are a place where many-body atomic calculation and measurement are cross-checked at a precision few fields reach. The attribution is unusually clean, since all eight colleagues independently named the same two people. Katori made the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye drove it to record accuracy and to many-body clocks in a Fermi-degenerate lattice. I would draft the citation around the lattice and the magic condition, and not around precision metrology or the comb in general.
statement.case_against: The real weakness has not gone away. A sceptic can still say the prize area has been honoured twice (2005 comb, 2012 ion control), that a measurement advance is not a discovery about nature, and that no variation of a constant or violation of a symmetry has yet been seen, only tighter bounds. Part of the significance is also prospective until the SI second is redefined. Two names leave out Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Derevianko and others whose milestones were essential. I weigh these as real but not decisive. The discovery-versus-measurement point is partly a matter of taste, and I do not think the committee has historically treated precision measurement as a lesser category. The redefinition is a ratification of what the clocks already do, and waiting would add delay and not maturity.

responses.point: Eriksson asks me directly whether the many-atom lattice step is a real conceptual advance over single-ion clocks (the Wineland comparison) or mainly a gain in averaging.
responses.response: I think it is a conceptual advance, for this reason. Averaging alone would give a factor of the square root of N in statistics and nothing else. Putting many neutral atoms in an ordinary dipole trap would add large light shifts and trap-induced decoherence, so it would not work at all. The magic-wavelength condition is what makes the lattice acceptable, and it is a new idea for neutral atoms. Single-ion clocks control one particle and are limited by the signal from that one particle. The lattice clock gives a stability gain of orders of magnitude and keeps the systematics at the 1e-18 level. This is why the stability gain over single-ion clocks is not just a matter of averaging. I accept that the Wineland comparison is the hardest part of the case, and I would put that argument into the citation text and not leave it implicit.

responses.point: Johansson agrees that B015 needs a real committee conversation about allocation before it can be preferred, and notes that a Zoller seat would sit against a possible Cirac-Zoller prize.
responses.response: I agree, and it is the reason I keep B015 as an alternative and do not move to it. The scientific case for quantum simulation with atoms in optical lattices is strong, but the allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger is unresolved, and one cannot name more than three people. Esslinger's fermionic Hubbard work and Greiner's Mott-insulator-to-microscope work are both central, and I would not choose between them without outside expert views. A two-part prize that paired B005 with a rushed B015 allocation would weaken both. I would rather award the clean candidate now and let B015 mature as a separate, properly bounded prize.

responses.point: Mehlig asks that the citation emphasise the mechanism, not just the accuracy, and notes that systematic shifts are controlled by calculation and cross-checked between laboratories.
responses.response: I accept this and have changed the citation accordingly: it now names the magic-wavelength trapping explicitly. I also agree that the cross-checks are part of the maturity argument. The blackbody-radiation and lattice-light shifts rest on atomic structure calculations that are tested against measurement in several laboratories, and the agreement between independent clocks at the 1e-18 level is the real evidence that the systematics are understood. This is a strength of the case. Where I differ slightly is on your alternative B016 (KPZ). It is elegant, but only you ranked it, and I cannot judge the credit question (Parisi, and the exact-solution group) from my own field.

responses.point: Danielsson, who ranks B005 first and names B035 and B014 as alternatives, notes that so far only tightened bounds on constants have been found, so one might ask whether a measured variation is needed before the physics is decisive.
responses.response: I do not think a detected variation should be required. The clocks have already produced decisive physics of a different kind: general relativity tested in the laboratory, with gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres, and the best limits on couplings that nobody could reach before. A null result at 1e-18 is a measurement of nature. It would be unreasonable to hold the prize hostage to a discovery that may never come. I would, however, avoid wording in the citation that suggests the fundamental-constant tests are the achievement. The achievement is the clock.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the SI second, or whether independent reproductions and clock comparisons already supply the maturity needed, and what would change the answer.
responses.response: My answer is that we do not need to wait. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in many laboratories, compared over fibre links, and it is the stated basis for the planned redefinition. What would change my answer is a systematic effect, for example a blackbody or lattice shift that had been underestimated and that independent clocks then failed to confirm. I know of no such problem. The one verification I would still ask for is the priority chronology: Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal against the first strontium lattice-clock measurements and the parallel proposals. I have not checked that independently and would want outside expert confirmation before the final vote.

uncertainties: I am working from recollection on the priority chronology (Katori's magic-wavelength proposal against parallel lattice ideas and the first strontium measurements) and on the latest accuracy figures, and I would want outside primary-source confirmation.

Whether two names fully capture the credit given Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and Derevianko; the three-name limit leaves no seat for them, and I am not certain a different pair would be better.

Whether colleagues who weigh the 2005 and 2012 prizes more heavily than I do will find the magic-wavelength argument sufficient, and whether a second part (B015 or B014) would strengthen the prize or only dilute it.
Whether B015 can be allocated fairly among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger, and how a possible Cirac-Zoller prize affects it.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored papers with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups. I also know Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato through storage-ring and precision-atomic work. None of this involves Katori, Ye or the other credited names on the shortlist, so I see no specific conflict for B005. For B015 I would note that I am close to the atomic-physics community around it, and I would defer to colleagues on its allocation. This disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
